posts.content_md:
Good day.

I'd like to try make ready-to-coat silver halide emulsion.

There is a recipe in the topic: [http://holographyforum.org/phpBB2/viewtopic.php?t=4591](http://holographyforum.org/phpBB2/viewtopic.php?t=4591)

but some things are not clear for me.

Here it goes:

> "In a method described by Lehmann, a solution of gelatin is first prepared as follows:A. Hard gelatin............20gWater....................390cc

By "hard gelatin" one means high-bloom gelatin ?

> This is dissolved and filtered though spun glass (glass wool) or cotton batting (wadding) and used at 35C.To 80cc of the A solution addDistilled water........10ccSilver nitrate............4gTo the balance of solution A, add and dissolve 3.2g of potassium bromide. Taking care that there is no froth on this, it is slowly poured into the gelatin-silver solution at the same temperature, stirring fairly gently during the precipitation and for three and one-half minutes afterwards.

So we divide our 4,87% gelatine solution into 2 parts: one is 80ml gelatine with DI water and silver nitrate, the other is c.a. 310ml of gelatine+KBr. And we add KBr to AgNO3 solution.

Jeff, what about reaction equilibrium when adding highly diluted KBr (0,96%) to a solution with predominance of Ag+ ions (AgNO3 concentration is 4,25%) ?

> The following sensitizing dyes are then added immediately:Pinacyanol (1:1000 alcoholic solution)........4ccOrthochrom T (1:1000 alcoholic solution)....4ccAcridin Orange (1:500 alcoholic solution)....4ccThis mixture of dyes must have been previously warmed to 30C. It is added slowly with gentle stirring, not more than forty-five seconds being taken. Under no circumstances must the emulsion be subjected to any further heating, the object being to avoid grain growth and fog formation.

I'd like to sensitize for red only - use 4ml of 1:1000 pinacyanol or 12 ml of 1:3000 solution ? I wouldn't ask if there wasn't the timing.

> A very thin coating is applied to glass which has been so perfectly cleaned that, if breathed upon, the condensation is even all over and clears quickly. The coated plates are laid on a cold slab to set, and are then washed in a trough with gently running water. Ten minutes should suffice to remove the potassium nitrate. The washed plates are best dried in a horizontal position. This is stated to give the most brilliant colors."

I guess mold coating is the way. Nothing about emusion thickness, though.

But what about unused emulsion (I will use some 10ml total) ?

If no further heating is allowed - could the emulsion be remelted after gelling ?

It would be a pity to throw away most of emulsion.

Has anyone of you tried this method ? How did it work ?

Jeff, will substituting KBr with LiBr help with getting smaller grain with this method ?

What about trying to pour the emulsion into (for example) liquid nitrogen to stop grain growth. After we gring our frozen gelatin and rinse it with cold (tap ?) water to remove silver nitrate traces. After rinsing we mix our AgBr/gelatin with water, heat it to 30-35deg.C and coat our plates.

I guess it's something similar to freeze-thawn process used by Slavich ?

Jean - you wrote you tried double-jet method - what were the results ?

Not necessarily compring to diffusion method.

Was your method similar to the one mentioned here ?

greetings & thanks

Adam

posts.author: Martin
posts.content_md:
> **glajciorz:** I guess mold coating is the way. Nothing about emusion thickness, though.

This is a formula for Lippmann photography. So this was meant to form a layer thickness in the 2um range. Moreover, silver concentration might be too low for a holographic emulsion. Furthermore, it might be difficult to do mold coating with a relatively low gelatin concentration such as this.

> But what about unused emulsion (I will use some 10ml total) ?If no further heating is allowed - could the emulsion be remelted after gelling ?It would be a pity to throw away most of emulsion.Has anyone of you tried this method ? How did it work ?

Yes, I've tried this method. Forming small “nano” grains isn't difficult – efficient spectral sensitization at good photo speed is the real challenge.

> What about trying to pour the emulsion into (for example) liquid nitrogen to stop grain growth. After we gring our frozen gelatin and rinse it with cold (tap ?) water to remove silver nitrate traces. After rinsing we mix our AgBr/gelatin with water, heat it to 30-35deg.C and coat our plates.I guess it's something similar to freeze-thawn process used by Slavich ?

Right. I've been told they were using several freezing/thawing cycles.

posts.author: Martin
posts.content_md:
> **glajciorz:** So why don't we use higher gelatin concentration (for example 10-15%) and higher silver concentration (for example 6-7%). Where is the catch ?

Grain growth. It's difficult to form ultra-fine grains at high gelatin/silver concentration.

> Did it work (for holography) ? What was the problem ?What about spectral sensitization - won't pinacyanol do it for us ?

The problem is, spectral sensitization without reduction/sulfur/gold sensitization provides speed levels in the DCG range only. Dye concentration is very crucial - too little or too much dye may actually desensitize the emulsion. 

> Martin, do you have detailed informations about this method ?Or about double-jet method ?

Regarding the freezing/thawing method, if you read German there's is a German patent, DE 1103760, (Schlossner, Adox Fotowerke, Verfahren zur Herstellung wasserarmer fotografischer Halogensilberemulsionen), which seems to have greatly inspired Kirilov/Vasilyeva/Zelikman (that is, the “Russian method”).
